Series::count_nonzero¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::count_nonzero() const
Series Series::count_nonzero(std::int64_t dim) const

What It Does¶

Counts how many elements are not exactly zero.

This is the reduction you reach for whenever a count of “hits” is the answer: how many predictions crossed a threshold, how many entries survived a mask, how sparse a weight matrix is, how many observations a row actually has. Because a boolean series stores true as 1 and false as 0, mask.count_nonzero() is simply “how many trues”, which makes it the natural partner of every comparison operator.

Two forms:

  • count_nonzero() returns a single int64 scalar — the count across the whole tensor.

  • count_nonzero(dim) counts along one axis and removes it, so a [rows, cols] input reduced over dim = 0 gives one count per column.

“Not zero” means exactly that: any value that does not compare equal to 0. NaN is not equal to 0, so NaN is counted. +/-inf are counted. -0.0 does compare equal to 0, so it is not counted. This differs from nonzero() only in what you get back — nonzero() returns the coordinates, count_nonzero() returns how many there are.

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t): the axis to reduce. Negative values count from the end. Omit it to count across the entire tensor.

Returns¶

Series An int64 count. The no-argument form returns a 0-D scalar. The dim form returns the input shape with dim removed (there is no keepdim).

Gradient¶

count_nonzero() is a discrete tally built on an equality test. It is not differentiable — a reverse pass through it alone raises the objective-is-disconnected guard.

Examples¶

Example 1. Across the whole tensor: three of the six entries are non-zero.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({{0.0, 1.0, 2.0}, {0.0, 0.0, 3.0}}).count_nonzero());

Output¶

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=3

Example 2. On the result of a comparison it becomes “how many satisfy the condition”.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-2.0, 0.0, 3.0, -1.0, 5.0, 0.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.gt(0.0).count_nonzero());

Output¶

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=2

Two values (3 and 5) are greater than 0.

Example 3. dim = 0 counts non-zeros down each column.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({
        {0.0, 1.0, 2.0},
        {0.0, 0.0, 3.0},
        {7.0, 0.0, 4.0},
    }).count_nonzero(0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 1, 3]

Column 0 has one non-zero (7), column 1 has one (1), column 2 has three.

Example 4. dim = 1 counts along each row instead.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({
        {0.0, 1.0, 2.0},
        {0.0, 0.0, 3.0},
        {7.0, 0.0, 4.0},
    }).count_nonzero(1));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2, 1, 2]

Example 5. NaN and inf are counted; -0.0 is not.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({
        std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(),
        -0.0,
        0.0,
        1.0,
        std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity(),
    }).count_nonzero());

Output¶

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=3

NaN, 1.0, and inf count; the two zeros (-0.0 compares equal to 0.0) do not.

Example 6. Integer and boolean inputs work the same way.

pluss::series::print(std::cout,
                     pluss::make_series({1, 0, 0, 2, 0, 3}).count_nonzero());

Output¶

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=3

Example 7. Negative dim counts from the end.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({{0.0, 1.0}, {2.0, 0.0}}).count_nonzero(-1));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 1]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • NaN counts as non-zero. If missing data is encoded as NaN, filter it first (e.g. x.isnan().logical_not()) or you will over-count.

  • Only exact zero is excluded. Tiny values like 1e-300 are non-zero; use a tolerance comparison (x.abs().gt(eps)) if “effectively zero” is what you mean.

  • The dim form removes the axis — there is no keepdim. To keep it, follow with unsqueeze(dim).

  • To count over several axes, either flatten first (flatten().count_nonzero()) or chain reductions.

  • Not differentiable.

Summary¶

count_nonzero() tallies the elements that are not exactly 0:

  • whole-tensor form gives an int64 scalar; count_nonzero(dim) reduces and drops one axis

  • mask.count_nonzero() is “how many trues”

  • NaN and inf count; -0.0 does not

  • not differentiable

See Also¶

  • Series::nonzero: the coordinates of the non-zero elements, not just how many.

  • Series::sum: mask.to(Int64).sum(dim) is the same count, and keeps a keepdim option.

  • Series::bincount: tally repeated integer values, not positions.

  • Series::any / Series::all: the yes/no questions count_nonzero() > 0 and count_nonzero() == numel().
